summary: Defines a way to describe and signal aspects of a digital identity transaction and its participants, such as how identity was proven and how the person authenticated, so a relying party can decide how much to trust it.

eli5.summary: Instead of just saying yes this is you, the answer comes with a score card of how it was checked.

questions: what do p1 cc ac mean in vot
what is the vot claim in openid connect
subtitle: A compact way for an identity provider to tell a relying party how a login was proofed, authenticated and delivered.

tldr.problem: A single Level of Assurance number is too coarse to describe a login, while full attribute metadata is too heavy for simple decisions.
tldr.mechanism: A vector is a period-separated string of components, each a letter plus a digit or lowercase letter, such as P1.Cc.Ac. It travels with a trustmark URL naming the trust framework that gives the values their meaning.
tldr.outcome: Relying parties get several separate signals instead of one score, and trust frameworks can define their own values. The RFC also defines default values and registers the OpenID Connect claims vot, vtm and vtr.

today: RFC 8485 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement or update. Its default values are meant for use when no more specific trust framework is available.

sections.title: Why a Vector
sections.content:
Trust in a digital login has usually been measured in one of two ways. One is a single scalar, the Level of Assurance (LoA), as in NIST SP 800-63 before its third edition. It is easy for a relying party (RP) to compare, but it cannot express cases like an anonymous account with a very strong credential, and one group's LoA2 is not comparable to another's. The other is detailed attribute metadata, which is expressive but forces the identity provider (IdP) to collect and send a lot of data.

Vectors of Trust (VoT) sits between the two. It expresses several independent aspects of a transaction without full attribute metadata. It is expected to be usable alongside attribute metadata systems, and some trust frameworks may map sets of vector values to LoAs for RPs that want less detail.
sections.eli5: A single grade like B+ does not tell you if a student is good at math or spelling. A report card with several subjects tells you more without being a whole essay.

sections.title: The Four Components
sections.content:
The RFC defines four orthogonal components, each named by a single uppercase letter, the demarcator. P is identity proofing, how strongly identity attributes were verified. C is primary credential usage, how strongly the credential can be verified, for example a password or a hardware device. M is primary credential management, covering binding, rotation and revocation. A is assertion presentation, how well the identity is communicated across the network without leaking or spoofing.

A value is the demarcator followed by one digit or lowercase letter. Categories with a natural ordering SHOULD use digits, with larger digits stronger; others SHOULD use letters. A component may repeat with different values in one vector, meaning a logical AND, but the same component and value MUST NOT repeat. An RP MUST NOT assume that a higher value implies a lower one without knowing the trust framework.
sections.eli5: The score card has four boxes: how well they checked who you are, how you unlocked your account, how the account is looked after, and how the answer was delivered.

sections.title: The Vector on the Wire
sections.content:
A vector is a period-separated list of components, such as P1.Cc.Cd.Aa. Order does not matter, so Aa.P1.Cd.Cc is equivalent, and the RP MUST treat them so. Omitted components make no claim: there are no placeholders and no default values are assumed.

A vector is meaningless alone, so it MUST be sent with a trustmark URL, cryptographically bound to it, for example by carrying both in one signed assertion. In OpenID Connect the IdP MUST send the vector in the vot claim of the ID token and the trustmark in the vtm claim. These apply to the whole transaction, and may also appear in a token introspection response.
sections.eli5: The score card is written as a short code, and the order of the boxes does not matter. It also says which rulebook explains the code.

sections.title: Requesting Vector Values
sections.content:
An RP can say which vector values it wants by using the same syntax. In OpenID Connect the client MAY send a vtr claim request whose value is a JSON array of strings. Components inside one string are ANDed together and the separate strings are ORed. For example, ["P1.Cb.Cc.Ab", "Ce.Ab"] accepts either the full first set or the full second set.

A request may omit components, meaning any value is acceptable for them. How the IdP maps the request to the login is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: The website can say what kind of score card it will accept, like asking for either of two recipes of checks.

sections.title: Trustmarks and New Values
sections.content:
A trustmark is an HTTPS URL that points to a human-readable document describing which components and values a trust framework allows and what practices they stand for. It MUST be reachable by the RP's operators and stable over time, and a new version of a framework that changes processing rules MUST use a different URL. The default values in the appendix use https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8485.

Extensions SHOULD reuse existing component categories and MAY register new demarcators in the registry. Trust frameworks MUST define all allowable values themselves, so P1 in one framework can differ from P1 in another. They MUST say whether multiple values are allowed per category, and use a unique trustmark URL. A 0 value is recommended for an empty condition.
sections.eli5: The trustmark is the address of the rulebook. Different rulebooks can use the same symbols to mean different things, so you must read the right one.

sections.title: Default Component Values
sections.content:
For use when no more specific framework exists, the appendix defines values. Proofing is ordered, and only one value may be used: P0 no proofing, P1 self-asserted but consistent attributes, P2 proofed in person or remotely by trusted mechanisms, P3 a binding relationship such as notarized documents or employment records.

Credential usage values (C0, Ca to Cg) range from no credential and session cookies to shared secrets, cryptographic key proofs, hardware tokens and local biometrics. Management has Ma, Mb and Mc. Assertion presentation has Aa to Ad, from an unsigned bearer identifier to an assertion encrypted to the RP's key. Multiple values may be combined in these three components.
sections.eli5: The default rulebook has simple levels: from no checking at all up to showing official papers, plus lists for how you logged in and how the answer was sent.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The vector must be protected in transit, for example with TLS, and tied to its trustmark, which a signed ID token does by carrying both as claims. An RP that does not understand a trust framework needs to reject its vectors, since reading a value in the wrong context could wrongly accept or reject a request. VoT only describes and conveys trust. It sets no policy for which values an IdP asserts or how an RP uses them, which IdP and RP must agree and document at the trustmark URL.

Vector values can reveal things about the user, such as that they were highly proofed or got a strong token. IdPs are advised to send, and RPs to request, only what the use case needs.
sections.eli5: A score card can give away secrets if it says too much, and it is useless if you read it with the wrong rulebook. So share only what is needed.

items.label: No proofing
items.desc: No proofing is done, and data is not guaranteed to persist across sessions.

items.label: Self-asserted
items.desc: Attributes are self-asserted but consistent over time, potentially pseudonymous.

items.label: Proofed
items.desc: Identity proofed in person or remotely using trusted mechanisms.

items.label: Binding relationship
items.desc: A binding relationship exists between the IdP and the identified party, such as notarized documents or employment records.
